name: Cockroach control
signs: Droppings, egg cases, a persistent odour or activity after dark can all be useful clues.
intro: Cockroaches can shelter close to warmth, food and moisture. Davis starts by finding where activity is occurring and what is helping it continue, then explains a treatment plan for the property.
assessment: An assessment looks at likely harbourage, food and moisture sources, access and the spaces in use. Share where and when you have seen activity; that detail can help identify the problem.
preparation: Preparation and re-entry advice depend on the treatment selected. Ask about children, pets, food preparation areas and any other site-specific concern before work begins.
faq: Should I spray the cockroaches I can see?
answer: Visible activity may be only part of the problem. Tell Davis what you have seen before using another product so the assessment can account for it.

name: Rodent control
signs: Scratching, droppings, gnaw marks, nesting material and disturbed stored food are common reasons to request an inspection.
intro: Rat and mouse activity needs more than a response to one sighting. Davis considers signs of activity, possible entry points and attractants before recommending control and prevention steps.
assessment: Describe where you hear or see activity and whether it is inside, outside or near stored food. The assessment can then focus on access, shelter and food sources.
preparation: Keep children and pets away from any control equipment as instructed. The appropriate placement, monitoring and proofing advice depend on the site.
faq: Will sealing a gap solve the problem on its own?
answer: Proofing can be important, but an active problem may need assessment and control as well. Davis can advise on the sequence after looking at the property.

name: Ant control
signs: Recurring trails, activity around food or ants entering through gaps can point to a wider problem.
intro: Ant activity may follow food, moisture and access routes around a building. Davis assesses the observed trail and the setting before recommending a suitable approach.
assessment: Note where ants appear, when the trail is active and whether the activity returns after cleaning. Those details help focus the inspection.
preparation: Treatment advice is specific to the property. Avoid disturbing an active trail before the visit if it can be left safely; it may help locate the source.
faq: Why do ants keep coming back?
answer: A visible trail can be connected to a source that has not yet been addressed. A site assessment is needed to decide what action makes sense.

name: Fly control
signs: Persistent indoor flies, repeated activity near windows or a suspected breeding source are reasons to investigate.
intro: Effective fly control begins with identifying the activity and possible breeding or entry conditions. Davis can review the site and discuss practical control and prevention options.
assessment: Share where flies gather, how often they appear and whether food, waste or drains are nearby. The site and type of activity shape the recommendation.
preparation: Sanitation, exclusion or maintenance may form part of the advice. Any treatment-specific preparation is explained before work is carried out.
faq: Is treating the visible flies enough?
answer: Often the source and entry conditions also matter. An assessment helps identify what should be addressed at the site.

name: Wasp control
signs: Concentrated flight paths, nest activity or repeated wasp presence near a building should be treated cautiously.
intro: A wasp nest can create a serious sting risk. Davis assesses the activity and the surrounding setting before advising on the safest practical next step.
assessment: Tell Davis where the activity is and whether people or pets use the area. You do not need to approach or disturb a suspected nest to describe it.
preparation: Keep clear of the suspected nest and follow the technician's site-specific instructions. Do not attempt to remove a nest yourself.
faq: Should I block the nest entrance?
answer: No. Disturbing or blocking a suspected nest can increase risk. Keep your distance and request professional advice.

name: Flea treatment
signs: Bites, pet scratching or small jumping insects around floors and furnishings may indicate flea activity.
intro: Flea management needs attention to the property, the life cycle and the animals that use the space. Davis explains preparation, treatment and aftercare for the specific situation.
assessment: Describe where activity is most noticeable and whether pets have been treated by a veterinarian. The property assessment helps determine the next step.
preparation: Preparation and aftercare matter. Follow the instructions given for the chosen treatment and coordinate pet care with your veterinarian.
faq: Why might I still notice fleas after treatment?
answer: The flea life cycle can affect what you notice afterwards. Davis can explain what to expect and when to follow up for the chosen treatment.

name: Spider control
signs: Recurring webbing, spiders around building edges or repeated activity in the same places can help locate the problem.
intro: Spider management depends on the species, the activity and the property. Davis reviews the places spiders shelter and what may be attracting their prey.
assessment: Point out recurring webs and the places where you have seen spiders. An inspection can consider building edges, sheltered spaces and associated insect activity.
preparation: Advice on cleaning, exclusion and any treatment is specific to the site. Tell Davis about pets and areas that need special care.
faq: Will removing webs stop spiders returning?
answer: Removing webs helps with housekeeping, but recurring activity may need a closer look at shelter and prey around the property.
